headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%

terms.meaning: The main interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The speed at which prices rise over time.
The group of nine experts at the Bank of England who vote on interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, from 3.75% to 4%, when its Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision on Thursday 5 November. Money markets put the chance of a rise at about 98%.
The expectation follows UK consumer price inflation rising to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, above the 3.4% that economists had forecast. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier and were the main driver. Britain is a net energy importer, so it is exposed to the energy shock linked to the conflict between the United States and Iran and disruption to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
At its September meeting the Bank held the rate at 3.75% by six votes to three, with three members already preferring a rise to 4%. Inflation data for September, published on 21 October, has pushed markets firmly towards a hike.
levels.why: A rate rise would make borrowing dearer for households and firms, but is meant to bring price rises back under control.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday 5 November. Financial markets see a rise of 0.25 percentage points as close to certain, at roughly a 98% chance.
The reason is inflation. Consumer prices were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, against a forecast of 3.4%. Petrol and diesel were nearly 30% more expensive, and Britain, which buys in much of its energy, is exposed to the oil shock linked to the US-Iran conflict and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted six to three to hold rates in September, with the three dissenters wanting a rise. The Bank's target is 2% inflation, so a figure of 3.5% leaves it under pressure to act, even though higher rates can slow growth.
levels.why: A rate rise would make borrowing dearer for households and firms, but is meant to bring price rises back under control.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday, lifting Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. Markets think a quarter-point rise is almost certain.
The main reason is that prices are rising faster again. Inflation reached 3.5% in the year to September, a little above what economists expected. Fuel prices were up almost 30% over the year, partly because the conflict involving Iran has disrupted oil supplies and pushed up the cost of energy, which Britain largely has to import.
The Bank wants inflation at 2%. Raising Bank Rate makes borrowing more expensive and saving more rewarding, which tends to cool spending and slow price rises. In September, three of the nine members of its rate-setting committee already wanted a rise, while six preferred to wait.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates on Thursday

levels.headline: Interest rates in the UK are expected to go up this week
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a bank that looks after the country's money. On Thursday it will probably raise the interest rate. That is the price of borrowing money. It would go from 3.75 to 4 out of every 100 pounds each year.
Why? Prices are going up too fast. Think of a bar of chocolate that costs more every few months. The Bank wants prices to go up slowly. Right now they are going up a bit too quickly. Petrol is much dearer than last year. Fighting in the Middle East has made oil cost more, and Britain has to buy a lot of its oil and gas from other places.
When borrowing costs more, people buy less, and prices calm down. But families with mortgages may have to pay more each month. Savers may get a little extra.
levels.why: If the rate goes up, borrowing costs more money, but prices should stop rising so fast.

levels.headline: Interest rates in the UK are expected to go up this week

Why is it doing this? Because prices keep going up. A loaf of bread or a litre of petrol costs more than it did last year. Petrol is nearly a third dearer. This is because of fighting in the Middle East, which has made oil cost more.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. Then prices stop rising so fast. But some families will pay more on their home loans, so it can be hard for them. People who save money may earn a bit more.
levels.why: If the rate goes up, borrowing costs more money, but prices should stop rising so fast.

levels.headline: Interest rates in the UK are expected to go up this week
levels.body:
Imagine you lend a friend some pocket money. You ask for a little extra back as a thank-you. That extra is called interest. The Bank of England sets how much extra people pay when they borrow money.
This week the Bank will probably make the extra a bit bigger. It does this because the price of things is going up too fast. Sweets, bus tickets and petrol all cost more than before. When borrowing costs more, grown-ups spend a bit less, and prices stop climbing so quickly.
But there is a catch. Families who borrowed money to buy a home may have to pay a bit more each month. So the Bank has to be careful. It wants to help without making life too hard for people. We will find out what it decides on Thursday.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.51% at 7,541.40 as Nasdaq falls 1.07% and Dow edges up
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.51% at 7,541.40 on Monday 2 November, the last completed US trading session. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07% to 25,164.32 as investors sold technology shares, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213.67 points, or 0.41%, to 51,983.98.
The split reflects a rotation out of technology and into more defensive sectors. October was the Nasdaq's worst month since March 2025, with a fall of 5.3%, while the Dow gained 1.7% over the same month. Late October's selloff followed weak Big Tech earnings that revived worries about AI spending.
Monday also saw oil prices drop sharply on hopes of renewed US-Iran talks, with Brent crude settling at $104.77. Tuesday's US session was still to open as this edition was prepared.
levels.why: Falling tech shares affect pension and savings funds, and show how nervous investors are about AI spending and the Iran conflict.

headline: Healey's first Budget raises £26.1bn in taxes, with a higher bank surcharge, gambling duty and property and savings tax rises

terms.meaning: An extra tax on bank profits, on top of normal corporation tax.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget raises £26.1bn in taxes, with a higher bank surcharge, gambling duty and property and savings tax rises
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October. The bank surcharge rises by three points to 6%, a temporary measure starting in January and ending 15 months later. Machine Games Duty goes from 20% to 25% for higher-stakes machines, with pubs and seaside arcades protected. Income tax rates on property and savings income rise by two points from April 2027, and there is a levy on properties worth over £2 million.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) put the tax rises at £26.1 billion of extra revenue by 2029-30. Healey says the plans meet the government's fiscal rules, though his borrowing buffer has shrunk to £15 billion from £24 billion.
The OBR now expects growth of 1.2% in 2026, slowing to 1.0% in 2027 as higher energy prices and interest rates bite, then 1.6% in 2028. Debt is forecast at 83.8% of GDP next year. UK 10-year gilt yields fell towards 5.3%, suggesting markets were largely reassured.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much tax people and firms pay and how much the government can spend, so it affects jobs, bills and public services.

headline: UK brings forward 3% defence spending target to 2030 and pledges extra £10bn for Ukraine

terms.meaning: A group of countries that have promised to help defend each other.
The total value of everything a country produces in a year.

levels.headline: UK brings forward 3% defence spending target to 2030 and pledges extra £10bn for Ukraine
levels.body:
In the 28 October Budget, Chancellor John Healey brought forward the date for the UK to reach defence spending of 3% of GDP, setting it at 2030. He also reaffirmed the NATO goal of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. The Office for Budget Responsibility projects defence spending of 2.6% of GDP in 2026-27, 2.7% in 2029-30 and 3.0% in 2030-31.
The Budget fully funds the £15 billion Defence Investment Plan, including £4.7 billion that was previously unfunded. Mr Healey also announced an additional £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, as well as urgent winter military funding.
The announcements came as Russian attacks on Ukraine continued and as European governments are asked to carry more of their own security costs.
levels.why: Defence spending competes with other priorities for public money, and decides how safe Britain and its allies are.

levels.body:

Analysts said much of the earlier price rise had been a risk premium, built up in anticipation of renewed fighting. Brent had ended October at its highest in six months, partly on fears that the conflict could flare after the US midterm elections.

levels.body:

Two of the 12 voters dissented, and both wanted a quarter-point rise: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack.
The statement said inflation remains elevated and that more information would help the Committee set a stance that returns inflation to 2%. The day after the decision, September's PCE inflation reading showed prices up 3.6% on a year earlier, slightly below the 3.7% expected but still well above target. Fed funds futures had priced in less than a 10% chance of a hike at the meeting, but nearly 75% expected at least one by year-end, with December the most likely date.
Chair Kevin Warsh said the economy is strong. The 10-year Treasury yield hovered below 5% after a strong GDP report. Barclays has suggested that persistent inflation could prompt consecutive quarter-point hikes in December and January.
